title: Asynchronous JS
body:
- Most real-world sites will consume web [[API]]s to get data
- It happens "outside" the  normal [[HTTP]] request / response. That is it happens on a seperate [[Thread]] 
```js
const url = "https://..."

//version 1 (not quite right)
const data  = fetch(url);
console.log(data);

//Version 2 (better)
fetch()
	.then (response => response.json())
	.then (data => {// do something with the data});
	console.log(data) 
	//undefined, because it hasn't happened yet, it's on some other thread
	//happening some time in the future.
```
`data` is a [[Promise]] object. and it's promise status would be `pending`
Using the [[Fetch]] function
[[Async Functions]]

[[Parallel Fetches]]


---

The mechanism underneath is the [[Event Loop]]: JavaScript has one thread of execution, and
`fetch` hands the actual network work to the browser, which calls your callback back once the
stack is empty. "It happens on a separate thread" is right about the network and slightly wrong
about your code, which never runs in two places at once. That is why a long synchronous loop
freezes the page and a pending fetch does not.

Three ways to write the same wait, in the order the course meets them: callbacks
([[Call Back Function]]), then [[Promise]] chains, then [[Async Functions]]'s `await`. Each is
sugar over the one before, not a replacement for it.
